title: Form and Function of Structures
seo_title: Grade 7 Science: Form and Function of Structures Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how the form of a structure relates to its function; identify internal and external forces and the centre of gravity; explain how materials, joints and shapes affect strength and stability; apply design criteria such as safety, cost, ergonomics, aesthetics and sustainability. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand D: Structures and Mechanisms – Form and Function)
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 science worksheets on form and function, forces on structures, stability, centre of gravity, materials, trusses and design criteria. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A structure's form must suit its function.
key_sub: Shape, materials, joints and a low centre of gravity make structures strong and stable.
body_html:
How to think about it

Every structure has a function (its job) and a form (its shape and size).

  • Internal forces: tension, compression, torsion and shear. External forces: loads such as weight, wind and snow.
  • Triangles, trusses, I-beams and arches add strength; a low centre of gravity and wide base add stability.
  • Designers balance function, safety, cost, ergonomics, aesthetics and environmental impact.
Example

Why are roof trusses made of triangles?

triangles are rigid

Answer: they do not change shape under a load

Example

Why do racing cars sit low?

low centre of gravity

Answer: for stability

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the strongest design is always the best (cost and weight matter too).
  • Thinking a taller structure is more stable.
  • Mixing up form and function.

faq.q: What is the difference between form and function?
faq.a: Form is the shape and size of a structure. Function is the job it does.

faq.q: How does the centre of gravity affect stability?
faq.a: A structure is more stable when its centre of gravity is low and over a wide base.
Designing products to fit the human body so they are comfortable and safe to use.

items.q: A tennis ball is hit back over the net. It changes direction. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: A rolling ball hits a wall. It stops or changes direction. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: Why do racing cars sit low to the ground?
c: A low centre of gravity keeps them stable in turns.
items.e: Low and wide is stable.

items.q: What is a frame structure?
c: a solid block like a dam
a structure made of parts joined together, like a skeleton
items.e: Houses and bicycles have frames.

items.q: A soccer ball is sitting still. A player kicks it. It starts moving. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: What is a truss?
c: a frame made of triangles that spreads loads
items.e: Many bridges and roofs use trusses.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the bricks at the bottom of a wall?
items.e: The bricks at the bottom of a wall: the weight above squeezes them, so it is compression (a squeezing or pushing force).

items.q: Why is an egg hard to crush when you squeeze its ends?
c: The curved shell spreads the force over the whole surface.
items.e: Curves spread loads.

items.q: Which shape is the weakest if pushed at a corner: a square frame or a triangle frame?
items.e: Squares can fold into a diamond shape.

items.q: A shelf bends under a load. Which change will reduce bending the most?
c: make the shelf thicker or add a support in the middle
move the books to the middle
items.e: Thicker beams resist bending.

items.q: A bike rider squeezes the brakes. The bike slows down. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: There are no forces at all.
Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: A hockey puck is hit with a stick. It speeds up. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?
c: Only gravity acts, so there is no answer.
There are no forces at all.
items.e: When motion changes (start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn), forces are unbalanced. When nothing changes, they are balanced.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a column holding up a roof?
items.e: A column holding up a roof: the roof pushes down on it, so it is compression (a squeezing or pushing force).

items.q: Which is a composite material?
items.e: Composites combine materials for better properties.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a bungee cord when someone jumps?
items.e: A bungee cord when someone jumps: it is stretched, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: What is universal design?
c: designing spaces and products that everyone can use, including people with disabilities
items.e: Ramps and automatic doors are examples.

items.q: Why are hockey helmets rounded?
c: A curved shell spreads the force of a hit.
items.e: The form fits the function: protection.

items.q: What is ergonomics?
c: designing objects to fit the human body comfortably and safely
items.e: Computer chairs and mice are ergonomic.

items.q: Why are snowshoes wide?
c: to spread the person's weight over a large area so they do not sink
items.e: Form matches function.

items.q: Why do tall buildings sway a little in strong wind?
c: They are designed to bend slightly instead of breaking.
items.e: Flexibility absorbs force.

items.q: Why do snowshoes help you walk on snow?
c: They spread your weight over a larger area.
items.e: Spreading a load reduces pressure.

items.q: Is weight a contact force or a non-contact force?
items.e: Gravity (weight), magnetism and electrostatic forces act at a distance; the others need contact.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the cables of a suspension bridge?
items.e: The cables of a suspension bridge: the cables are pulled tight, so it is tension (a pulling or stretching force).

items.q: A ball on the floor is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the floor pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: Is air resistance a contact force or a non-contact force?
items.e: Gravity (weight), magnetism and electrostatic forces act at a distance; the others need contact.

items.q: Which natural structure is a shell?
items.e: Turtle shells are curved and strong.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a wet towel being wrung out?
items.e: A wet towel being wrung out: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: Why do bridges have expansion joints?
c: To make the bridge longer every day
Materials expand in summer heat and shrink in winter cold.
items.e: Joints stop cracking.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a key turning in a lock?
items.e: A key turning in a lock: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: A book on a shelf is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the shelf pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a shelf sagging under heavy books?
items.e: A shelf sagging under heavy books: it is pushed down in the middle, so it is bending (a mix of compression and tension that bends a material).

items.q: A rock on the ground is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the ground pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: A lamp on a desk is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: Gravity pulls it down and the desk pushes it up with an equal force.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: What happens if a structure's load is greater than it can hold?
c: It may bend, crack or collapse.
items.e: Engineers add a safety margin.

items.q: What is the name of the upward push of a liquid or gas on an object in it?
items.e: Learn the names of common forces.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a bolt holding two sliding plates together?
items.e: A bolt holding two sliding plates together: the plates push it sideways in opposite directions, so it is shear (two forces pushing in opposite directions across a material).

items.q: What is a dynamic (live) load?
c: a load that changes or moves, like traffic or wind
the weight of the roof beams
items.e: Dynamic loads change.

items.q: A box on a bench is not moving. Which statement is true?
c: The forces on it are unbalanced.
Gravity pulls it down and the bench pushes it up with an equal force.
items.e: An object at rest still has forces on it. They are balanced.

items.q: What is the name of the force that slows things down when surfaces rub together?
items.e: Learn the names of common forces.

items.q: Why is the base of the CN Tower wide?
c: A wide base makes it more stable against wind.
items.e: Wide bases resist tipping.

items.q: Which is an external force on a house?
items.e: External forces act on a structure from outside.

items.q: A boat is moving and there is a net force forwards. What happens?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: A soccer ball is still and there is a net force to the left. What happens?
c: It starts to move to the left.
It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: The cart is at rest. What will happen?
c: It will move to the left.
It will move to the right.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change the motion of an object at rest.

items.q: Why does a chair have four legs spread apart?
c: To stop it from being sat on
A wide base makes it stable.
items.e: A wide base keeps the centre of gravity over it.

items.q: Why is steel rebar put inside concrete?
c: Steel resists tension, so the concrete does not crack when it bends.
items.e: Reinforced concrete is strong both ways.

items.q: A cardboard bridge sags under a toy car. How could you make it stronger?
c: fold the cardboard into a corrugated or triangular shape
items.e: Shapes add strength.

items.q: What is a structure?
c: something built to hold or support a load
items.e: Buildings, bridges, chairs and nests are structures.

items.q: What is a design brief?
c: a statement of the problem, the criteria and the constraints for a design
items.e: Engineers start with a brief.

items.q: A boat is still and there is a net force to the left. What happens?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
It starts to move to the left.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: Why are triangles used in roof trusses?
c: Triangles are rigid and do not change shape under a load.
items.e: A triangle can only change shape if a side bends or breaks.

items.q: Which bridge design uses an arch to carry loads by compression?
c: a suspension bridge with no towers
items.e: The arch pushes loads to its ends.

items.q: The crate is at rest. The arrows show two forces. What will happen?
c: It will move up into the air.
It will start to move to the left.
It will start to move to the right.
items.e: The bigger force points to the left, so the forces are unbalanced and the crate moves that way.

items.q: The wagon is at rest. What will happen?
c: It will move to the left.
It will move to the right.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change the motion of an object at rest.

items.q: The box is at rest. The arrows show two forces. What will happen?
c: It will start to move to the right.
It will move up into the air.
It will start to move to the left.
items.e: The bigger force points to the right, so the forces are unbalanced and the box moves that way.

items.q: A cyclist is still and there is a net force to the left. What happens?
c: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
It starts to move to the left.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.q: What is the purpose of a factor of safety?
c: to make a structure stronger than it needs to be in case of extra loads
items.e: Bridges are built to hold more than normal traffic.

items.q: What does 'form' mean when describing a structure?
items.e: Form must suit the function.

items.q: Why are hockey sticks often made of carbon fibre?
items.e: Materials are chosen for their properties.

items.q: Which material is strong in compression but weak in tension?
items.e: Concrete is reinforced with steel bars (rebar).

items.q: Which internal force acts on a diving board with a swimmer at the end?
items.e: A diving board with a swimmer at the end: the top stretches and the bottom squeezes, so it is bending (a mix of compression and tension that bends a material).

items.q: How can you make a paper column hold more books?
items.e: Tubes resist compression well.

items.q: Which internal force acts on paper being cut by scissors?
items.e: Paper being cut by scissors: two forces push in opposite directions across it, so it is shear (two forces pushing in opposite directions across a material).

items.q: What is a shell structure?
c: a thin, curved outer layer that holds its shape
items.e: Eggs, domes and canoes are shell structures.

items.q: What should engineers think about when building a structure?
c: safety, strength, cost, the environment and how it will be used
items.e: Good design balances many criteria.

items.q: Why are suspension bridge towers so tall?
c: Tall towers hold the main cables that carry the deck's weight in tension.
items.e: Cables pull up on the deck.

c: a dam that is thicker at the bottom
items.e: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom.

c: No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
items.e: Count both: 5 and 5. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Which design factor is about how a product looks?
items.e: Aesthetics is about appearance.

items.q: Why are triangles used in bridges and towers?
c: Triangles are always made of wood.
Triangles keep their shape and spread forces well.
items.e: A triangle cannot be pushed out of shape without bending its sides.

items.q: Ava took apart building A and built B. Could Ava have used all the same blocks?
c: No. A looks taller, so it has more blocks.
No. B looks bigger, so it has more blocks.
No. Blocks disappear when you take them apart.
items.e: Count both: 10 and 10. Same pieces, new shape.

items.q: Why are I-beams used in buildings?
c: Their shape is strong while using less material.
They are made of wood only.
items.e: The flanges resist bending.

items.q: Chloe says B was built from all the blocks in A. Is that true?
c: Yes. They are both made of blocks.
No. A has 6 blocks and B has 7.
Yes. B is a new shape, so it must be the same.
items.e: Count the blocks in each building.

items.q: What is the centre of gravity?
c: the point where all of an object's weight seems to act
items.e: A low centre of gravity improves stability.

items.q: Which internal force acts on the stones of an arch bridge?
items.e: The stones of an arch bridge: the arch pushes the stones together, so it is compression (a squeezing or pushing force).

items.q: What is a load?
c: a force acting on a structure, such as weight, wind or people
items.e: Structures must carry loads.

items.q: Why does a heavy snowfall worry owners of flat roofs?
c: The extra load could make the roof collapse.
items.e: Snow is a big load in Ontario winters.

items.q: Why should engineers think about the whole life of a product?
c: to reduce waste and environmental harm from making, using and throwing it away
because it is the law in every country
items.e: Sustainable design looks at the full life cycle.

items.q: How could you check that a spring stretches in proportion to the force?
c: Add all the weights at once.
Use a different spring each time.
Add equal weights one at a time and measure the extension each time.
items.e: Fair test.

items.q: Ava wants to test how the size of a push changes how far a ball rolls. What should she change?
c: only the size of the push
items.e: Change one variable for a fair test.

items.q: What is a foundation?
c: the base that spreads a building's load into the ground
items.e: Foundations stop buildings from sinking.

items.q: Does a car moving at a steady speed on a flat road need a net force?
c: No. The driving force balances friction and air resistance.
items.e: Newton's first law.

items.q: Ava pushes a toy car gently and then hard. Which push makes it move farther?
items.e: A bigger force changes motion more.

items.q: Why does a ship float?
c: Water pulls it up with magnets.
The upthrust from the water balances its weight.
items.e: Balanced forces.

items.q: What is a static (dead) load?
c: a load that does not change, like the weight of the structure itself
items.e: Static loads stay the same.

items.q: What is a constraint in a design challenge?
c: a limit, such as cost, time or materials
items.e: Constraints limit possible solutions.

items.q: Why do astronauts bounce around on the Moon?
c: There is no gravity at all.
Their weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
The Moon is made of springs.
items.e: Weaker gravitational field.

items.q: What is a solid structure?
c: a structure made of solid material all the way through
items.e: Dams and brick walls are solid structures.

items.q: Jayden hangs a weight from a spring. The spring stretches, then stops. Why does the weight stop moving?
c: The spring pulls up with the same force as gravity pulls down.
items.e: The forces become balanced.

items.q: Which structure is a solid structure?
items.e: Solid structures are filled all the way through.

items.q: A skydiver falls at a steady speed. What can you say about the forces on her?
c: Weight is much bigger than air resistance.
Air resistance is bigger than weight.
Her weight and the air resistance are balanced.
items.e: Terminal velocity.

items.q: A steel beam has a heavy load in the middle. Which part is in tension?
items.e: The top squeezes and the bottom stretches.

items.q: Which structure is a frame structure?
c: a hydro tower made of steel beams
items.e: Frames are joined parts with spaces between.

items.q: Which internal force acts on a screwdriver turning a screw?
items.e: A screwdriver turning a screw: it is twisted, so it is torsion (a twisting force).

items.q: Why is it safer to put heavy items on the bottom shelf?
c: It lowers the centre of gravity so the shelf is less likely to tip.
items.e: Low centre of gravity improves stability.

items.q: A sled is sliding down a snowy hill. A friend pulls it from the bottom with a rope. What happens?
items.e: The pull is opposite to the motion, so it slows the sled.

items.q: Noah pushes a heavy box but it does not move. Why?
c: Friction pushes back with the same force, so the forces are balanced.
items.e: Balanced forces do not change motion.
